questions.q: Which mature cell is derived from the common lymphoid progenitor rather than the common myeloid progenitor?
questions.explanation: Natural killer cells share the common lymphoid progenitor with B and T cells; megakaryocytes, neutrophils, and monocytes are myeloid.

questions.q: Which precursor-product relationship is shown in the blood-cell lineage tree?
questions.explanation: Circulating monocytes can enter tissues and differentiate into macrophages.

questions.q: Which organ is identified as a major source of complement proteins?
questions.explanation: The liver synthesizes many circulating complement proteins.

questions.q: Which structure filters lymph and provides a site for immune-cell encounters?
questions.explanation: Lymph nodes filter lymph and organize interactions among antigens and immune cells.

questions.q: Which property belongs to innate immunity rather than adaptive immunity?
options: Broad recognition with little time lag
questions.explanation: Innate immunity responds rapidly and recognizes broad microbial patterns rather than specific antigens.

questions.q: Which component is classified as an internal innate defense on the response map?
questions.explanation: Natural killer cells are internal innate effectors; antibodies and cytotoxic lymphocytes are adaptive.

questions.q: Which pairing correctly matches an adaptive branch with its principal effector?
questions.explanation: The humoral adaptive response is mediated by antibodies, whereas the cell-mediated branch uses cytotoxic lymphocytes.

questions.q: Which mechanical defense removes inhaled particles from the respiratory tract?
questions.explanation: Coordinated ciliary movement transports mucus and trapped particles out of the airways.

questions.q: Which antimicrobial enzyme is found in both tears and saliva?
questions.explanation: Lysozyme in tears and saliva damages susceptible bacterial cell walls.

questions.q: Normal flora protect a body surface primarily by competing with pathogens for:
questions.explanation: Competition for nutrients and attachment space creates antagonism or colonization resistance.

questions.q: Which listed blood component functions mainly as an intercellular communication signal?
questions.explanation: Cytokines are secreted signals that coordinate immune-cell behavior.

questions.q: Which pair consists mainly of adaptive immune lymphocytes?
questions.explanation: B and T lymphocytes are the principal cellular components of adaptive immunity.

questions.q: Which white blood cell is strongly associated with release of mediators that promote inflammation?
questions.explanation: Mast cells release inflammatory mediators and are important in immediate inflammatory responses.

questions.q: Approximately what fraction of circulating white blood cells is made up of neutrophils according to the slide?
questions.explanation: The slide identifies neutrophils as the most abundant WBC population at roughly 50–60%.

questions.q: What is the membrane-bound compartment formed immediately after a phagocyte engulfs a microbe?
questions.explanation: Engulfment encloses the microbe in a phagosome.

questions.q: Where does most enzymatic killing and digestion of an engulfed bacterium occur?
questions.explanation: Fusion of the phagosome with lysosomal/granule compartments creates the degradative phagolysosome.

questions.q: Neutrophil granules principally store which class of effector molecules?
questions.explanation: Granules provide rapidly deployable enzymes and antimicrobial proteins for microbial killing.

questions.q: The structural scaffold of a neutrophil extracellular trap is primarily:
questions.explanation: NETs are extracellular DNA-rich webs decorated with antimicrobial proteins.

questions.q: What is the immediate defensive function of a NET?
questions.explanation: NETs immobilize microbes and concentrate antimicrobial molecules around them.

questions.q: Approximately what percentage of circulating WBCs is represented by monocytes on the slide?
questions.explanation: The slide gives monocytes as approximately 2–10% of WBCs.

questions.q: What happens to many monocytes after they leave the bloodstream and enter tissues?
questions.explanation: Tissue entry is followed by differentiation of monocytes into macrophages.

questions.q: Which macrophage function directly helps activate antigen-specific T-cell responses?
questions.explanation: Macrophages can display processed antigen to T cells, linking innate uptake to adaptive activation.

questions.q: Which statement correctly classifies natural killer cells?
questions.explanation: NK cells are lymphoid in lineage but function as innate immune cells and are neither B nor T cells.

questions.q: Which surface molecule on a normal host cell commonly supplies an inhibitory signal to NK cells?
questions.explanation: Normal expression of MHC class I engages inhibitory NK receptors and restrains killing.

questions.q: The term “missing self” refers most directly to reduced expression of:
options: MHC class I on a target cell
questions.explanation: Virus-infected and transformed cells may lose MHC class I, removing an inhibitory NK-cell signal.

questions.q: Which NK-cell granule protein promotes entry of granzymes into the target cell?
questions.explanation: Perforin facilitates delivery of granzymes, which initiate apoptotic death.

questions.q: Granzyme entry into an NK-cell target most directly triggers:
questions.explanation: Granzymes activate intracellular death pathways that cause apoptosis of the target cell.

questions.q: In granule-mediated cytotoxicity, what occurs immediately before polarized granule release?
questions.explanation: The cytotoxic lymphocyte first recognizes and binds its target, then directs granules toward the contact site.

questions.q: Cytotoxic T cells recognize target cells through specific binding to:
questions.explanation: A cytotoxic T-cell receptor recognizes a specific peptide displayed by MHC class I.

questions.q: What does virulence describe?
options: The host's capacity to make antibodies
The ability of a drug to dissolve clots
A pathogen's capacity to harm its host
questions.explanation: Virulence is the degree or capacity of a pathogen to cause host damage.

questions.q: Which combination best captures the slide's distinction between a microbe and a pathogen?
questions.explanation: Virulence factors equip a microbe to enter, persist, evade defenses, damage the host, or spread.

questions.q: Which process enables a bacterium to persist despite active host defenses?
questions.explanation: Immune-evasion mechanisms allow bacteria to avoid recognition, killing, or clearance.

questions.q: Which event is most directly responsible for the clinical manifestations of bacterial disease?
options: Tissue damage by toxins or direct microbial effects
Receptor absence from a non-target tissue
questions.explanation: Disease signs and symptoms arise when toxins or direct microbial activities damage host tissue.

questions.q: During bacterial adherence, the receptor is generally located on the _____ and the ligand on the _____.
questions.explanation: Adherence commonly involves a microbial ligand or adhesin binding a receptor on the host cell.

questions.q: M protein is a virulence factor associated with:
questions.explanation: M protein is a major surface virulence factor of Group A Streptococcus.

questions.q: Which host extracellular-matrix protein is specifically linked to M-protein-mediated adherence and invasion?
questions.explanation: Binding to fibronectin promotes attachment to and invasion of epithelial and endothelial cells.

questions.q: Host specificity of an adherent pathogen is strongly influenced by:
options: Distribution of the matching host receptor
questions.explanation: A pathogen can efficiently attach only where its adhesin's matching receptor is available.

questions.q: Where is a bacterial capsule located?
questions.explanation: A capsule is an external layer surrounding the bacterial cell wall.

questions.q: Which organism is listed as an encapsulated bacterial example?
questions.explanation: The slide lists S. pneumoniae, H. influenzae, and B. anthracis as capsule-bearing examples.

questions.q: TLR4 is shown recognizing which bacterial PAMP?
questions.explanation: TLR4 is a pattern-recognition receptor for bacterial LPS.

questions.q: How can a capsule reduce innate immune recognition?
options: By producing host MHC class I
By converting T cells into macrophages
questions.explanation: The capsule can physically conceal microbial patterns from host pattern-recognition receptors.

questions.q: What is the main effect of a capsule on phagocytosis?
options: It reduces phagocyte attachment and engulfment
questions.explanation: Capsules hinder effective contact between a phagocyte and the bacterial surface.

questions.q: Which surface coating can restore efficient recognition of an encapsulated bacterium by phagocytes?
questions.explanation: C3b is an opsonin; phagocytes bind it through complement receptors to improve engulfment.

questions.q: A capsule can promote intracellular survival after engulfment by increasing resistance to:
questions.explanation: Some capsules protect engulfed bacteria from digestion by lysosomal enzymes.

questions.q: Quorum sensing allows bacteria to alter gene expression in response to:
questions.explanation: Accumulating signaling molecules let bacteria estimate local cell density and coordinate gene expression.

questions.q: What best defines a biofilm?
questions.explanation: Biofilms are structured microbial communities, usually attached to a surface and embedded in a matrix.

questions.q: Which bacterial enzyme directly targets a mucosal antibody?
questions.explanation: IgA protease cleaves secretory IgA and helps pathogens evade mucosal immunity.

questions.q: Which pair of enzymes primarily promotes spread through connective tissue?
questions.explanation: Hyaluronidase and collagenase digest connective-tissue components and facilitate invasion.

questions.q: Which enzyme-organism association is correct?
questions.explanation: C. perfringens produces collagenase, supporting deep-tissue spread in gas gangrene.

questions.q: Hyaluronidase is listed for both Staphylococcus aureus and:
questions.explanation: The slide associates hyaluronidase with S. aureus and S. pyogenes.

questions.q: How does coagulase help Staphylococcus aureus evade host defenses?
options: It promotes a clot-like protective barrier
questions.explanation: Coagulase-driven clot formation can shield bacteria from phagocytes, immune factors, and antibiotics.

questions.q: What is the clinical use of streptokinase stated on the slide?
options: Dissolving blood clots during heart attacks
questions.explanation: Streptokinase is a thrombolytic enzyme used to dissolve clots.

questions.q: Peptidoglycan is composed principally of:
questions.explanation: Peptidoglycan is a mesh-like polymer containing sugar chains cross-linked by short peptides.

questions.q: Mycolic acid contributes to virulence chiefly by increasing resistance to:
questions.explanation: The mycolic-acid-rich wall helps mycobacteria withstand lysosomal degradation.

questions.q: Invasin-triggered membrane ruffling allows microbial entry by rearranging:
questions.explanation: Invasins trigger signaling that reorganizes the host actin cytoskeleton and drives membrane engulfment.

questions.q: What is toxigenicity?
options: The capacity of a phagocyte to ingest bacteria
The ability of a microorganism to produce toxins
The presence of toxin in blood
The host response to a capsule
questions.explanation: Toxigenicity denotes toxin-producing ability.

questions.q: What does toxemia mean?
options: Presence of toxins in the blood
Presence of bacteria in a biofilm
questions.explanation: Toxemia specifically refers to circulating toxin in blood.

questions.q: How does diphtheria toxin enter a host cell?
questions.explanation: After receptor binding, the toxin is internalized by receptor-mediated endocytosis.

questions.q: Diphtheria toxin fragment A halts translation by ADP-ribosylating:
questions.explanation: Modification of the diphthamide residue of eEF-2 prevents protein elongation.

questions.q: Which receptor is bound by the B pentamer of cholera toxin?
questions.explanation: The five B subunits bind GM1 receptors and promote toxin internalization.

questions.q: Cholera toxin causes persistent activation of adenylyl cyclase by locking which protein in its active GTP-bound state?
questions.explanation: The A1 fragment modifies Gsα, causing persistent adenylyl cyclase activity and high cAMP.

questions.q: How many transmembrane helices characterize a typical GPCR?
questions.explanation: GPCRs contain seven membrane-spanning alpha helices.

questions.q: A ligand-bound GPCR directly activates which intracellular signaling component?
questions.explanation: The activated receptor promotes nucleotide exchange and activation of a heterotrimeric G protein.

questions.q: Which intrinsic activity of Gα helps terminate GPCR signaling?
questions.explanation: Gα hydrolyzes bound GTP to GDP and returns to its inactive state.

questions.q: Which combination produces receptor-level attenuation after prolonged GPCR activation?
options: BAX activation and cytochrome c release
questions.explanation: Phosphorylation enables arrestin binding, which uncouples the receptor from further G-protein activation.

questions.q: The toxic portion of Gram-negative lipopolysaccharide is:
questions.explanation: Endotoxin activity resides in the lipid A component of LPS.

questions.q: Which process can release endotoxin from Gram-negative bacteria?
questions.explanation: Bacterial breakdown by complement, phagocytes, or antibiotics can release LPS/endotoxin.

questions.q: Which host molecules mediate many systemic effects after endotoxin recognition?
questions.explanation: Endotoxin induces inflammatory cytokine secretion, which contributes to fever and systemic inflammation.

questions.q: Which response is most directly associated with endotoxin exposure on the slide?
questions.explanation: Endotoxin is pyrogenic and promotes inflammatory cytokine-driven fever.

questions.q: Why may killing Gram-negative bacteria fail to make a preparation endotoxin-free?
options: Lipid A is converted into peptidoglycan
Sterilization creates living spores in all cases
Endotoxin can remain after bacterial death
questions.explanation: Endotoxin is a heat-stable bacterial component that may persist even when bacteria have been killed.

questions.q: A substance that induces fever is termed a:
questions.explanation: Endotoxins are pyrogens because they can induce fever.

questions.q: Which is a homeostatic function of programmed cell death?
options: Removal of damaged or infected cells
Permanent inhibition of all cell turnover
questions.explanation: Programmed death removes unwanted, damaged, stressed, or infected cells and helps maintain tissue balance.

questions.q: Which feature is biochemical rather than morphological evidence of apoptosis?
questions.explanation: Caspase activation is a biochemical hallmark; the other options are visible morphological changes.

questions.q: Which membrane change marks an apoptotic cell for phagocytic clearance?
questions.explanation: Phosphatidylserine exposure on the outer leaflet acts as an engulfment signal.

questions.q: Which pair contains only executioner caspases?
questions.explanation: Caspases 3, 6, and 7 are executioners; caspases 8 and 9 are initiators.

questions.q: Caspase cleavage of cytoskeletal regulatory proteins contributes directly to:
questions.explanation: Caspase-dependent reorganization of cortical actin contributes to apoptotic surface blebs.

questions.q: Cleavage of phospholipid-transfer proteins during apoptosis causes surface exposure of:
questions.explanation: Disrupted phospholipid asymmetry exposes phosphatidylserine on the cell surface.

questions.q: Which proteins directly permeabilize the mitochondrial outer membrane during intrinsic apoptosis?
questions.explanation: Activated BAX and BAK oligomerize in the outer mitochondrial membrane and permit cytochrome c release.

questions.q: Cytochrome c release promotes assembly of which caspase-activating complex?
questions.explanation: Cytosolic cytochrome c drives apoptosome assembly and activation of initiator caspase-9.

questions.q: Which BCL-2 family classes are BH3-only proteins?
questions.explanation: BH3-only activators and sensitizers contain only the BH3 homology domain.

questions.q: Which BCL-2 family groups possess BH1–BH4 domains?
questions.explanation: Multi-domain effectors and anti-apoptotic BCL-2 proteins contain all four BH domains.

questions.q: Which adaptor protein is recruited to activated Fas receptors?
questions.explanation: FADD links clustered Fas death receptors to procaspase-8 within the DISC.

questions.q: Which initiator caspase is activated in the Fas-associated DISC?
questions.explanation: The extrinsic pathway activates initiator caspase-8 at the DISC.

questions.q: Which condition commonly favors necroptosis over extrinsic apoptosis?
questions.explanation: Necroptosis is often engaged when death-receptor signaling occurs but caspase-8-dependent apoptosis is blocked.

questions.q: Which morphology distinguishes necroptosis from apoptosis?
options: Cell shrinkage with intact blebbing membrane
questions.explanation: Necroptosis is lytic, with cytoplasmic swelling, swollen mitochondria, and membrane rupture.

questions.q: Which receptors can serve as extrinsic triggers of necroptosis?
questions.explanation: The slide lists TNFR1 and the pattern-recognition receptors TLR3 and TLR4 as extrinsic triggers.

questions.q: Intrinsic necroptosis can begin when ZBP1 recognizes:
questions.explanation: ZBP1-dependent recognition of Z-nucleic acids is shown as an intracellular trigger.

questions.q: Which molecules released by necroptotic cells alert immune cells to tissue damage?
questions.explanation: Lytic membrane rupture releases damage-associated molecular patterns, or DAMPs.

questions.q: Which cells are specifically listed as detecting necroptosis-derived DAMPs?
options: T cells, dendritic cells, and macrophages
questions.explanation: The slide names T cells, dendritic cells, and macrophages as DAMP-responsive immune cells.

questions.q: What activates many lysosomal degradative enzymes?
questions.explanation: The acidic lysosomal lumen turns on multiple degradative hydrolases.

questions.q: Which cathepsins are stated to be abundant in lysosomes?
questions.explanation: Cathepsins L, B, and D are listed at high lysosomal abundance.

questions.q: What type of molecular damage defines ferroptosis?
questions.explanation: Ferroptosis results from iron-dependent accumulation of phospholipid hydroperoxides.

questions.q: Which enzyme is a major defense against phospholipid hydroperoxide accumulation?
questions.explanation: GPX4 reduces phospholipid hydroperoxides and suppresses ferroptotic membrane damage.
